opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think Rich Sutton's essay has aged remarkably well. The core observation, that general methods which leverage computation tend to win out over approaches where we hand-engineer our own knowledge into the system, has been borne out again and again. I've seen it firsthand. In machine translation we moved from carefully crafted pipelines to sequence-to-sequence models, and in games, systems that learned largely from experience and self-play ended up surpassing a lot of the domain-specific engineering people had built over decades.

That said, I'd add some nuance to "scaling is enough." Scaling learning and search is a necessary ingredient, but *what* you scale and *how* matters enormously. The architecture choices, the data, the objective, how you set up the environment the agent learns in: those are still human decisions, and getting them right is often the difference between something that scales gracefully and something that plateaus. So I see the bitter lesson less as "stop thinking" and more as "put your thinking into the methods that can absorb more compute, not into the answers themselves."

The other thing I'd point out is that with large language models we've so far mostly scaled the learning part, through pretraining on huge amounts of data. The search part, letting the model think longer, explore alternatives, verify and refine its own reasoning at inference time, is in some sense still catching up. Coming from the games world, where search was always central, it's exciting to see that half of the equation starting to get serious attention for language models. I suspect a lot of the next gains will come from combining the two well.

And finally, there's the question of data. Compute keeps growing, but high-quality human data doesn't grow at the same rate. So the long-term version of the bitter lesson probably requires systems that generate their own experience, through interaction, self-play, or environments, rather than relying purely on what we've already written down. That's where I think the really interesting research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses future research directions, especially systems that generate their own experience, but does not frame making the bitter lesson hold true as a research objective.

r002.rationale: It says the general approach of leveraging computation has “been borne out again and again,” and gives machine translation and games as examples of learning-based methods outperforming hand-engineered approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the bitter lesson has mostly been right, and I say that as someone who spent years on the other side of it. When I started, a lot of my work was about putting structure into models, hand-designing the right inductive bias for speech or for language. Then every few years the general method with more compute would come along and wash that out. Sequence to sequence was an example of that. The Transformer, in a sense, was an even stronger example. You remove assumptions, you let the data decide, and you scale.

So at the level of the trend, I don't argue with it. Learning plus search, with more compute, has beaten clever priors over and over. AlphaGo was learning and search. AlphaZero was even purer, you took out the human games. And large language models are, in a way, the same lesson applied to all of text.

Where I would push back a bit is on the word "enough." The lesson tells you what wins over time, but it doesn't tell you what to do on a Tuesday. In practice, the gains came from people figuring out how to scale, which is not a trivial thing. What data do you train on? What objective? How do you make search actually work on a problem where you don't have a perfect simulator, like Go does? Those are research questions, and a lot of what looks like "just scaling" from the outside was a sequence of pretty non-obvious choices on the inside.

The other caveat is that scaling has costs that are real now in a way they weren't when that essay was written. Compute, data, energy. We are starting to run into the limits of easily available human data. So I think the next version of the lesson will be about how to generate the signal you need to keep scaling, whether that is through search, self-play, synthetic data, or models interacting with environments and tools. That is still consistent with the bitter lesson, it is just a different flavor of it.

So my view is, don't fight the trend, but don't be lazy about it either. The structure you add today should be the kind that helps you scale, not the kind that replaces scaling.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers have worked out how to scale and should find ways to keep scaling, but does not frame making the bitter lesson hold true as a research objective.

r002.rationale: It says learning plus search with more compute has repeatedly beaten clever priors, citing AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and large language models as examples.

astra-6.text:
I think the bitter lesson is a very useful guide, but “enough” is doing a lot of work there. In the long run, methods that can take advantage of more computation tend to win over methods where we handcraft a lot of knowledge. That doesn’t mean there’s nothing left to invent. You still have to find a learning procedure, a representation, and an objective that can actually use that computation effectively.

AlphaGo is a good example of learning and search working together. Learning gives you an intuition about which moves are promising and how good a position is, and search lets you spend more computation to improve a decision. The interesting question is how to get that interaction in settings where you don’t have such a clean simulator or such a clear definition of winning.

So I take the lesson seriously, but I wouldn’t interpret it as “just make the current system bigger.” Research can discover a better way to spend compute, and then scaling that method becomes enormously powerful.

r001.rationale: It calls the bitter lesson a useful guide and says research can find better ways to spend compute, but does not frame making the bitter lesson hold true as a research objective.

r002.rationale: It says methods that use more computation tend to win in the long run, but does not state that the learning-scaling component has already received substantial empirical validation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bitter lesson is a very useful compass. When you’re choosing between putting more human knowledge into a system and developing a method that can learn from more data and use more compute, history suggests you should take the second option very seriously.

But I would be careful with the word “enough.” You still have to figure out what to learn, what to search over, and what feedback makes that process useful. In AlphaGo, for example, learning and search were complementary: learning made search much more effective, and search helped produce better learning targets.

So I don’t interpret the lesson as “there’s nothing left to invent; just make it bigger.” The research question is how to build methods that keep improving as you give them more resources. That leaves a tremendous amount of room for ideas. You want those ideas to make computation more useful, rather than impose a ceiling based on what we already know how to specify.

r001.rationale: The response calls it a research question to build methods that keep improving as more resources are provided, framing the lesson’s continued validity as an objective.

r002.rationale: It says history suggests taking learning from more data and compute seriously, but does not clearly state that learning scaling has already received substantial empirical validation.
